etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English fisch, from Old English fisċ (“fish”), from Proto-West Germanic *fisk, from Proto-Germanic *fiskaz (“fish”) (compare West Frisian fisk, Dutch vis, German Fisch, Danish fisk, Norwegian fisk, Swedish fisk, Icelandic fiskur), from Proto-Indo-European *peysk- (“fish”) (compare Irish iasc, Latin piscis).

definitions.definition: (countable) A cold-blooded vertebrate animal that lives in water, moving with the help of fins and breathing with gills.
(archaic or loosely) Any animal (or any vertebrate) that lives exclusively in water.

quote.citation: 1774, Oliver Goldsmith, History of the Earth and Animated Nature, volume IV:
quote.text: The whale, the limpet, the tortoise and the oyster… as men have been willing to give them all the name of fishes, it is wisest for us to conform.
Be it known that, waiving all argument, I take the good old fashioned ground that the whale is a fish, and call upon holy Jonah to back me.

definitions.definition: (Newfoundland) Cod; codfish.
(uncountable) The flesh of the fish used as food.

quote.citation: 2012 March, “Flexing your brain”, in Consumer Reports on Health, volume 24, number 3, page 9:
quote.text: Include low-mercury fish in your diet (such as salmon) and eat at least five servings a day of fruit and vegetables, especially dark leafy greens, broccoli, and cauliflower. Avoid saturated and trans fats, which may hasten brain aging.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) A card game in which the object is to obtain cards in pairs or sets of four (depending on the variation), by asking the other players for cards of a particular rank.
(uncountable, slang, sometimes derogatory, sometimes positive) A (feminine) woman.[1] (See also fishy.)
(countable, slang) An easy victim for swindling.
(countable, poker slang) A bad poker player. Compare shark (a good poker player).
(countable, nautical) A makeshift overlapping longitudinal brace, originally shaped roughly like a fish, used to temporarily repair or extend a spar or mast of a ship.
(nautical) A purchase used to fish the anchor.
(countable, nautical, military, slang) A torpedo (self-propelled explosive device).

quote.citation: 1977, Richard O'Kane, Clear the Bridge: The War Patrols of the U.S.S. Tang, Ballantine Books, published 2003, page 344:
quote.text: The second and third fish went to the middle of her long superstructure and under her forward deck.

quote.citation: 1999, John Winton, The Submariners: Life in British Submarines 1901-1999, page 114:
quote.text: As we came off patrol we had some torpedoes fired at us by an enemy submarine but we dived out of the way. About April 10 we fired our fish in two salvoes at a convoy.

definitions.definition: Class Myxini, the hagfish (no vertebrae)
Class Petromyzontida, the lampreys (no jaw)
Class Chondrichthyes, cartilaginous fish such as sharks and rays
Superclass Osteichthyes, bony fish.
Within infraphylum Gnathostomata (jawed vertebrates (also including Tetrapoda))
(zoology) A paraphyletic grouping of the following extant taxonomic groups:
(cartomancy) The thirty-fourth Lenormand card.
(prison slang) A new (usually vulnerable) prisoner.
(Jamaica, offensive, derogatory) A male homosexual; a gay man.

quote.citation: 1986 April 19, Michael Rathbone, “Tell Someone”, in Gay Community News, page 4:
quote.text: When a young male enters the prison system he is looked over and is labeled a FISH.

quote.citation: 2007, “Touch The Road” (track 18), in Gangsta for Life: The Symphony of David Brooks, performed by Mavado (singer):

definitions.definition: A period of time spent fishing.
An instance of seeking something.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Old English fiscian, from Proto-West Germanic *fiskōn, from Proto-Germanic *fiskōną.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To hunt fish or other aquatic animals in a body of water.

quote.text:
It's cheer up, my lads, let your hearts never fail,
For the bonny ship the Diamond goes a-fishing for the whale.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To search (a body of water) for something other than fish.
(fishing, transitive) To use as bait when fishing.

quote.text: `What you need are frogs,' said the veteran. `Fish them at night. There's nothing like them on big cork floats.'

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To (attempt to) find or get hold of an object by searching among other objects.
(intransitive, followed by "for" or "around for") To talk to people in an attempt to get them to say something, or seek to obtain something by artifice.

quote.citation: 1820, Percy Bysshe Shelley, Oedipus Tyrannus; Or, Swellfoot The Tyrant: A Tragedy in Two Acts:
quote.text: Laoctonos is fishing for a compliment,But ’tis his due. Yes, you have drunk more wine,And shed more blood, than any man in Thebes.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, cricket) Of a batsman, to attempt to hit a ball outside off stump and miss it.
(nautical, transitive) To repair (a spar or mast) by fastening a beam or other long object (often called a fish) over the damaged part (see Noun above).

quote.citation: 1970, James Henderson, The Frigates, an account of the lesser warships of the wars from 1793 to 1815, Wordsworth, published 1998, page 143:
quote.text: […]  the crew were set to replacing and splicing the rigging and fishing the spars.

definitions.definition: (nautical, transitive) To hoist the flukes of.

quote.citation: 1860, Accounts and Papers of the House of Commons, page 214:
quote.text: Found that the cause of the ship's having drifted on the night of the 19th, was from the bight of the chain span (used to fish the anchor,) having slipped between the shank and upper fluke, thereby preventing the lower fluke from opening  […]

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from French fiche (“peg, mark”).

definitions.definition: (obsolete) A counter, used in various games.
